Drought and water demand in Peru's river basins

How often each of Peru's 231 hydrographic units is in severe drought today, how that changes with +2 °C and +4 °C of global warming, and how much water is licensed in each basin, by sector. Drought is measured with SPEI, which counts both rainfall and the evaporative demand of the atmosphere.

Map by basin

Severe drought: SPEI-12 at or below −1.5. Future SPEI uses the distribution fitted to 1991-2020, so it reads as "as dry as a severe drought of today's climate". Runoff change is not shown for basins with under 20 mm of runoff per year.

Where demand and drought meet

Each point is a basin (hyper-arid coastal units excluded). Right of the dashed line: the third of basins with the most licensed consumptive water use (≥ 62 hm³/yr). Point size: water licensed to mining. Thick outline: priority basins.

Data and method

Climate: TerraClimate v1.1 (Abatzoglou et al., 2026; CC0), monthly at about 4 km, 1958-2025, and its +2 °C and +4 °C pseudo-warming versions. Evaporative demand is Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration. Basins and water rights: National Water Authority (ANA): 231 hydrographic units and the water use rights in force, summed per basin and sector. Hydropower, aquaculture and fishing are not counted as consumptive.

SPEI follows Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010) with a log-logistic distribution fitted per basin and calendar month on 1991-2020 (xclim).

Limitations

The +2 °C and +4 °C series apply one pattern of change to the observed record: they do not show the spread between climate models. TerraClimate runoff comes from a simple water balance without glacier melt or inflow from upstream basins and is well below gauged flows in Pacific basins, so it is used only as a relative change, never as available water. Licensed volume is the volume a right allows, not the volume used.
